promptLatex: In how many ways can $9$ distinct labeled towns be connected by roads so that every town can be reached from every other one and town $1$ is joined by a road to exactly one other town?
hintLatex: Encode each network by its Prüfer code, a sequence of length $n-2$ built by repeatedly deleting the smallest leaf and recording its neighbor.
A town joined to exactly one road is a leaf, which is equivalent to its label never appearing in the code.
So the code has length seven over the other eight labels, giving $8^7$ possibilities.
solutionLatex:
The networks described are trees on $9$ labeled vertices. Each corresponds to exactly one Prüfer code of length $9-2 = 7$: repeatedly delete the smallest leaf and record its neighbor, stopping after seven deletions.

A town is joined to exactly one road precisely when it is a leaf, and a vertex is a leaf exactly when its label is absent from the code. So the condition on town $1$ is that $1$ never appears in a code of length $7$ over the remaining eight labels. Each of the seven positions has $8$ choices, giving $8^7$ codes, and since the correspondence is a bijection the count of networks is the same:

$8^7 = 2097152$.

Sanity check: Cayley's formula gives $9^{7} = 4782969$ trees in total, and a tree on nine vertices has at least two leaves, so $2097152$ being a bit under half of that is what one should expect.
